Explaining and Investigating RPM Software Packages
All software from Red Hat comes as
Think of a flat-pack furniture box with a parts list and instructions. An RPM holds the files to install, facts about them (
: name, version, what other packages it needs, and more), and small scripts that run on install or removal. A local
records every installed package, so removal is clean.
An RPM is files plus metadata plus scripts, tracked in a database.
A package name has four parts: name, version, release and architecture.
It is like a product label: what it is, which edition, which print run, and which kind of machine it fits. The file form is
. The version comes from the original authors; the release is set by the packager.
If several versions exist, the higher version is installed. With equal versions, the higher release wins.

Red Hat signs every package with a
(a digital seal), and RPM refuses a package whose seal does not match.
It is like a tamper-proof seal on a medicine bottle: if the seal is broken or wrong, you do not use what is inside. RPM checks the seal before it installs anything.
A wrong signature means RPM will not install the package.
An update replaces the old package with a complete new one.
It is like swapping an old appliance for a new model instead of patching the old one. Config files are usually kept, but the packager decides. Normally only one version is installed. The
(the core of the operating system) is the exception: several versions can sit side by side, so an old one can still boot if a new one fails.
Updates replace packages; only the kernel keeps several versions.

5.5 Enabling a stream and installing a module
Installing a module enables its stream if needed and installs its default profile.
Think of picking a version line, then ticking an install preset. If you give no stream or profile, yum uses the defaults. You can also enable a stream by hand with
default stream and installs its default profile.

Only one stream can be enabled for a module. Enabling another stream disables the first one.

5.6 Removing a module and disabling a stream
Removing a module does not disable its stream; do that as a separate step.
It is like clearing the furniture without closing the shop.

removes the packages installed by the enabled stream's profiles, and anything that depends on them. Packages not in any profile stay and must be removed by hand. The stream stays enabled until you disable it.

Removing modules and switching module streams can be tricky. Switching the stream is the same as resetting the current stream and enabling the new one; it does not change installed packages automatically. Installing a different stream directly is not recommended, because upgrade scripts might break things and cause data loss or configuration problems.
